title: Proxy edge serialization & p99 breakdown - Aurora Ventures deep dive
summary: SE-led deep dive investigating p95/p99 spikes tied to edge proxy serialization, TLS/HTTP2 multiplexing, and VPC egress; explored streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, KV cache hotkeys, and batching strategies. Agreed next steps: run a short benchmark with HTTP gRPC vs HTTP2+keepalive, collect tcpdump from edge, and test a quantized model profile in a dedicated pool.
topics: KV cache hotkey behavior and sharding
VPC egress path and network hop analysis
action_items: Owen Park: collect tcpdump + edge proxy logs and share with Redwood by 2026-08-03
Ruth Chang: run micro-benchmarks (http2 vs grpc, streaming vs non-streaming) and upload results by 2026-08-05
Samir Patel: share security & network topology checklist and Redwood Dedicated perf sheet by 2026-08-02
next_steps: Customer to provide example requests and a short sample traffic replay
Run bench: small quantized model on dedicated pool vs hosted real-time streaming
Schedule follow-up to review tcpdump and results (week of 2026-08-09)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-30 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Samir, Ruth, Diego (Redwood); Lena, Marco, Priya, Owen (Aurora)

---
Summary (auto): SE deep dive into p95/p99 latency spikes. Focus on proxy serialization and network hop variance; clarified streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs and KV cache patterns.

---
[00:00] Samir (Redwood AE): All right everyone, thanks for joining. we've got a one hour plus deep dive focused on the p95/p99 spikes you saw last week. Ruth will drive the technical stuff and Diego will help with bench details. quick round of intros?
[00:17] Lena (Aurora): Hey Samir, hi team. I'm Lena, CTO. Marco will walk through the SRE observations after I give a quick bit of context.
[00:26] Marco (Aurora SRE): yep. we saw recurring p99s around 420–560ms on some routes, while p50 stayed ~40ms. spikes corresponded to mid-day traffic bursts.
[00:37] Ruth (Redwood SE): ok and these are for the streaming endpoint or the non-streaming synchronous calls?
[00:44] Marco: mostly the streaming endpoints, but some synchronous requests also saw blips. we thought batching would help but it's inconsistent.
[00:51] Ruth: got it. a few quick hypotheses: proxy-edge serialization (we've seen extra serialization when the edge does header manipulation), HTTP2 multiplexing stalls, TLS renegotiation at the proxy, and KV cache hotkeys or cross-shard fetches. also, streaming vs non-streaming changes the packetization and egress patterns.
[01:11] Owen (Aurora Net): to add, our edge uses an L7 proxy with some custom lua filters that add headers for tenant routing. there could be per-request locking there.
[01:22] Diego (Redwood): also worth checking keep-alive window sizes and Nagle interactions — tiny writes during streaming can get delayed if not using TCP_NODELAY.
[01:34] Lena: hmm we haven't tuned those since setup. we also have a sidecar that signs requests, could that be it?
[01:41] Ruth: yes sidecar signing introduces a small CPU cost per request; if it serializes IO it can amplify latency under burst. but we usually see that as a steady offset, not spiky p99s. spikes point to head-of-line blocking somewhere.
[01:53] Marco: here are the three patterns we logged: (1) cold-cache first token with KV miss goes to backend and returns ~350ms, (2) streaming frames pause for 200–400ms mid-stream, (3) isolated TLS renegotiation events correlated with a control-plane rollout.
[02:11] Samir: ok let's decompose pattern (2) — streaming frames pause. is it always at the same frame index or random?
[02:18] Marco: mostly early in the stream, 2nd–4th frames. not consistent across clients.
[02:25] Ruth: that smells like a proxy buffer fill or head-of-line due to reordering or blocking on an out-of-band call — maybe a KV refresh. do you see requests to a KV store around that time?
[02:36] Priya (Aurora): yes our platform issues a synchronous KV lookup for tenant policies on the first request. it's then cached for 30s.
[02:43] Diego: caching TTLs that short can create stampedes at scale. also hotkey behavior: if one tenant is super chatty and all requests go to same shard, you get queueing at the KV node, which shows up as intermittent p99.
[02:56] Owen: our KV is sharded by tenant so a hot tenant will concentrate traffic. but the weird thing is the pause occurs even when the KV call returns quickly.
[03:03] Ruth: could be synchronous io on the critical path — if the request blocks waiting for signature + KV + proxy header enrich, the streaming engine can't flush frames. streaming usually helps because it keeps the token pipeline moving, but if the preamble is synchronous, you still get a big initial tail.
[03:19] Samir: another angle: serialization/deserialization cost between proxy and runtime — e.g., we saw systems do JSON encode/decode at the proxy, or copy-heavy grpc wrappers that allocate a lot. those copies can spike latency unpredictably.
[03:34] Lena: we do UTF-8 header normalization and an odd rewrite step; it's possible.
[03:38] Marco: any thoughts on HTTP2 vs gRPC? we use HTTP2 with some gRPC-esque calls but it's effectively HTTP2 frames.
[03:45] Ruth: gRPC multiplexing helps when you have many simultaneous streams on a single connection, but it can also lead to head-of-line if the peer stalls or if prioritization isn't used. HTTP/1.1 with many short connections has TLS handshake cost but avoids stream multiplex stalls. for low p99 you often want a persistent connection tuned with keepalive and flow control.
[04:06] Diego: practical test: run the same traffic using true gRPC over HTTP2 with flow-control tuning and with an alternative path using independent TLS connections (HTTP/1.1 or http2 but different conn) to see if multiplexer stalls correlate.
[04:18] Owen: we can replicate that — but we'll need to instrument per-connection RTT and per-stream stats. we can pull cps from envoy metrics.
[04:25] Ruth: yes envoy has per-stream counters and per-connection write stalls; also look at envoy's buffered_bytes and downstream_flow_control_paused.
[04:34] Marco: we didn't track buffered_bytes previously. good call.
[04:38] Samir: on the model side, quantization can change CPU vs GPU time. a quantized model may run faster per-token on GPU, but if your runtime spills to CPU for certain ops or uses int8 kernels with slower memory patterns you can get unexpected latency variance. did you test quantized profiles?
[04:58] Priya: we tried a quant-mode off-the-shelf and saw slightly lower cost but p99 stayed noisy.
[05:04] Ruth: likely because the network and proxy are dominating; until you eliminate the edge serialization you won't see the model delta. let's separate concerns: first fix network/proxy path, then measure model quant impact.
[05:16] Marco: agreed. what bench should we run?
[05:19] Diego: small repro plan: (A) replay representative traffic to a Redwood test endpoint with tcpdump at edge, (B) toggle streaming vs non-streaming, (C) compare grpc multiplexing vs isolated connections, (D) run with sidecar signing enabled/disabled. send us the sample traffic and we'll set up a bench harness.
[05:34] Owen: timeline?
[05:35] Samir: if you can share traffic by Tuesday we can have initial bench by the end of week.
[05:40] Marco: yes we can share.
[05:41] Ruth: a few other low-level items to capture: TCP keepalive settings, TFO (if used), socket buffer sizes (sndbuf/rcvbuf), and whether the proxy is doing request coalescing or buffering. also check whether the sidecar uses synchronous file reads (e.g. reading certificate files per request). those sometimes slip in.
[06:02] Lena: noted.
[06:04] Samir: let's dig into the proxy serialization idea — Ruth, do you want to walk through common sources of serialization cost?
[06:10] Ruth: sure. first: header transformations that do many string allocations; second: JSON path rewrites; third: protocol translation (HTTP1->HTTP2 translation) that copies payloads; fourth: websocket or streaming reassembly doing small buffer copies. every copy allocates and can cause GC or CPU spikes.
[06:26] Marco: our proxy has a lua filter for header edits which runs in the main thread — maybe it's blocking.
[06:32] Ruth: that would explain early-frame pauses. lua filters are convenient but can introduce sync work on the data path. suggestion: move header enrich into an async enrich pipeline or pre-warm the policies so the enrich is a table lookup.
[06:47] Owen: for per-tenant signing we do a sync call to a local process that holds a key. maybe move to an in-memory signer or cache signatures for very short TTLs.
[06:57] Diego: yes signing per request is ok if it is cheap; otherwise batch signing or use a shared long-lived token for a short window.
[07:05] Ruth: also, check gRPC compression settings — compressed frames are CPU-heavy on decode and can add jitter if CPU is contended.
[07:13] Lena: we turned on gzip compression at the proxy layer to save bandwidth. that may be hurting.
[07:17] Samir: compression on short messages often hurts latency; disable for small streaming frames.
[07:22] Marco: good catch. we'll test with compression off.
[07:25] Ruth: next, KV hotkeys: if a tenant hot shard is saturating the KV, consider client-side sharding or caching shards at the proxy layer with a local LRU to avoid synchronous roundtrips for policy.
[07:39] Priya: we do have an LRU at the proxy but it's small and TTL is short.
[07:44] Diego: bumping the cache size or using a small per-worker local cache can remove roundtrips for the first few frames.
[07:50] Owen: is prefix/KV caching supported on Redwood side?
[07:53] Ruth: Redwood supports prefix/KV caching in the serving runtime; caching at the edge and runtime together can be complementary, just watch invalidation.
[08:04] Samir: practical experiment: have the proxy return a synthetic cached policy client-side and see if early-frame pauses disappear. if yes, we found the culprit.
[08:12] Marco: ok we'll try that.
[08:14] Ruth: about batching: continuous batching tries to accumulate tokens across concurrent sessions before firing a batch to the model. it's great for throughput but if the batch wait timer is too long you get increased p95. you can tune the batch wait (max latency) and min_batch_size. we typically suggest conservative batch wait for low-p99 environments.
[08:31] Diego: and batching interacts with streaming because streaming flushes partial tokens earlier — streaming lowers p50 but can increase tail if you rely on batch bundling.
[08:40] Marco: so the knobs are: batch size, batch wait time, and whether to prefer streaming partial flushes.
[08:46] Ruth: correct. also look at dynamic batching rules based on route or tenant. e.g., for low-latency tenants, disable batching or set very low wait. for high-throughput tenants, allow larger batch windows.
[08:59] Lena: what about model quantization tradeoffs here? if quant reduces GPU time but increases CPU copy time, could that make p99 worse?
[09:07] Ruth: yes if quantized kernels have worse memory access patterns or if the runtime does extra unpacking, you can add variance. but again network/proxy often dominates. after we remove edge stalls, we can test quantized profiles with warm caches and consistent batching.
[09:21] Marco: another angle: VPC egress and NAT gateway saturation. we have bursty NAT allocations that sometimes route via a different AZ and add 10–50ms.
[09:31] Owen: we've seen ephemeral NAT port exhaustion cause new flows to be routed differently which changed RTTs.
[09:36] Diego: capture flow logs and SNAT table churn. also test pinning to dedicated egress IPs or using regional load balancers to avoid cross-AZ hairpins.
[09:47] Ruth: good. if routing changes are happening mid-stream that would show as packet reordering and cause head-of-line. capture per-packet traces.
[09:55] Samir: ok recapping diagnostic plan: get tcpdump & envoy metrics, toggle compression, disable lua filter temporarily, simulate cached policy, compare gRPC multiplexing vs isolated connections, and run quantized vs fp bench after network fixes.
[10:11] Marco: noted. any quick wins to mitigate now?
[10:14] Ruth: disable compression for small frames, raise proxy local cache size, and temporarily disable sync signing to test impact. these should be low-risk.
[10:23] Lena: we'll try those in a staging cluster first.
[10:27] Ruth: one more micro-optimization: prefer HTTP/2 SETTINGS tweaks — increase initial window size and stream-level window to reduce flow-control stalls for early frames.
[10:38] Owen: we'll surface those to infra team.
[10:40] Diego: for benching, we'll provide a harness that can replay real traffic (we'll need headers scrubbed for PII) and produce p50/p95/p99 breakdowns plus per-component latency (proxy, signer, KV, runtime).
[10:54] Marco: are there Redwood console metrics we can correlate?
[10:58] Samir: yes we'll add per-route traces in Redwood Console, include model invocation start/end, and show prefix cache hits. we'll share a dashboard template.
[11:06] Priya: about security/compliance, if we move signing to a shared token that reduces per-request security posture; any guidance?
[11:13] Samir: short-lived tokens issued by a KMS-backed auth service are common — you get both performance and security. Redwood Private supports integration with customer KMS and HSM if you want to keep keys on-prem.
[11:25] Lena: good to know.
[11:27] Ruth: last question from my side: do you use an edge TLS termination or passthrough?
[11:32] Marco: termination at the proxy then mTLS to backend.
[11:35] Ruth: that adds extra crypto CPU; check whether hardware TLS offload or using a faster cipher suite helps. also ensure session resumption is properly configured to avoid full handshakes.
[11:47] Owen: we did see occasional full handshakes during control-plane rollouts.
[11:51] Samir: ok that maps to the pattern (3) you mentioned. ensure connections are drained and new connections smoothly ramp. Redwood can help with a canary rollout policy for runtime mutations.
[11:59] Marco: perfect.
[12:01] Samir: great. let's capture owners and dates. Owen will collect tcpdump and envoy metrics by Aug 3. Ruth will run bench and provide results Aug 5. Samir will send security/arch doc and Redwood Dedicated perf sheet Aug 2. we'll meet the week of Aug 9 to go over results.
[12:20] Lena: thanks all. any final Qs?
[12:23] Priya: one small ask — can Redwood share a concise checklist for proxy tuning?
[12:28] Samir: yes we'll send a short checklist with the notes we discussed: disable small-frame compression, increase http2 window, raise cache sizes, check lua filters, and pin egress.
[12:40] Marco: thanks.
[12:42] Samir: thanks everyone. ending now.

---
Post-call notes: Customer agreed to run the suggested toggles in staging. Redwood to provide bench harness and a pre-built dashboard. several low-risk mitigations (disable compression, increase cache, temp disable signer) prioritized as immediate steps.
